THE MINES REGULATION BILL.

THE debates in committee on the Mines
Regulation Bill are so strange, that they
require some explanation. Mr. BaucE intro-
duced a Bill which was, upon the whole,
satisfactory to the miners. In the interval
between the second reading and the committee,
a conference took place between certain repre-
sentatives of the mine-owners and the miners,
in which the latter were induced to assent to
two amendments proposed by the former,
which went far to nullify the value of the
Bill. By the first of these the word
"knowingly" was to be inserted in several
places. The result of this would be that it
would be almost impossible to obtain a con-
viction against a mine-owner for employing
young persons illegally. When Mr. &wee,
most highly to his credit, opposed the amend-
ment, member after member stood up to urge
that it was desired by the miners themselves,
inasmuch as it had been agreed to by their
representatives at the conference. Eventually
Mr. BRUCE was beaten by 185 to 170. The
representatives of the miners will probably
say that they submitted to this amendment
because they did not feel strong enough to
resist it. But the smallness of the majority
shows clearly that it would never have been
carried against Government if the men's own
representatives had not furnished members
with a pretext for supporting it.

There can be no doubt that this amendment
is dead against the interest of miners. Mr.
BRUeR has since deliberately expressed his
opinion that "its effect is to reduce an impor-
tant clause to a nullity, and deprive young
persons employed in mines of the protection
which it is most desirable to extend to them."
Mr. BRUCE has been severely blamed in past
years for supineness in this matter. I believe
I lave myself used strong language about him.
But here we find him fighting the battle of the
miners without the support which ho had a
right to expect.
A similar scene took place in the House on
Tuesday last. The miners' representatives
had consented to another amendment inserting
the words "under ordinary circumstances" in
the first of the general rules in clans() 48.
The effect of this would be that it would
practioelly impossible to obtain a conviction
against any mine owner for the insufficient
ventilation of his mine. Mr. Rarcr, firmly
resisted the amendment, and again he was met
by the assertion that the miners themselves
were in favour of it, inasmuch as thcir repre-
sentative had agreed to it. Fortunately it was
defeated, and the miners are deeply indebted
to Mr. BR= for saving them from the results

Too deep an interest cannot be taken in the
proceedings of Mr. DISRAELI just now. Or-
dinarily his speeches refer to accidental and
temporary circumstances. Every word he
utters now is meant to skilfully prepare the
way for his anticipated accession to office.
For years his rhetorical efforts have been only
training exercises. Now he is about to
throw his hat into the ring, and therefore every
step is measured, every guard prepared, and
every joint and muscle lubricated, that when
grappling with his opponent he may strike,
parry, and struggle with adroitness and force.
There is much pleasure in watching his graceful
movements, and examining the skilful man-
ceuvres by which ho seems to be preparing
himself for his final spring. He, however,
somewhat overdoes his part; he feints, and
doubles, and dodges, advances, and draws
back, until the patience:of the on-lookers begins
to give way, and they are disposed to cry out
with IlifaLET, "leave thy damnable faces and
begin."
The Manchester speech and the Church
School speech were full of Mr. DISRAELI'S
strength and weakness. The Crystal Palace
display did not differ from these in kind,
though it did to some extent in character. It
was not less clever, but it was far less.effec-
tive. Had it been the first of the three, it
would have been the best, being the last,
apart from its surroundings, it was the worst,
simply because the tricks by which the orator
produces his effects, and the repetitions of
ornamental comrnon•place caused his acting
to be more easily and more generally seen
through. His assurances that the Tory party
deserved their overthrow in the past, it must
be admitted, required some little courage when
made to such an audience; but his explan-
ation that this was owing to the Tories of past
generations " permitting their party system to

THE STRIKE AND LOCK-
OUT IN THE LONDON
BUILDING TRADES.

INTRODIJOTION.

The strike and lock-oat seem destined to run
their course, neither party showing any readiness
to offer terms of conciliation. On the contrary,
every step taken tends to widen the breach, and
each side proclaims itself to be confident of

victory.
The carpenters seem to hava discovered that
there may be too much even of parliamentary
government. On Saturday night the ordinary
delegate meeting was omitted, and the executive
pushed forward financial business. The committee,
observing the bad effect of holding at arm's-length
all the other branches of the building trade, have
taken a bold and candid step for correcting the
err or. On Saturday they issued invitations to the
other branches of the trade whioh have organized
themselves to send delegates to a general meeting.
This friendly overture distinctly states that future
united action is one of its objects. While central-
ising in one direction, the carpenters are decentral-
ising in another. Within the past few days they
have established local committees in a number of
districts, and these will greatly relieve the central
COMM Mee as far as routine work is concerned.
The Masons' Committee say that men having
been locked out a fortnight, they are ablelo form
some estimate of their position. After reviewing
that position in a calm and dispassionate Manner
they had come to the conclusion that it was•
very favourable, and that everything gave pro-
mise to success if the men only acted in tha same
firm and prudent way as heretofore. They urged
upon all not te.throw away any advantage they now
possessed by acts of violence which would bring
them within the provisions of the Criminal Law
Amendment Act—an Act bristling with traps to
catch and punish the working man, but at the
IMMO time possessed of wonderful elasticity in rela-
tion to employers.
The masons had been advised to form
themselves into a Co-operative Building Company,
purchase sites of land in the metropolis, and build
houses for themselves and their fellow workmen.
Apparently, however, one very important fact
must be remembered—the enormous difference in
price of land in Edinburgh and in London. In
the former place it was obtained for a nominal
sum; in the latter it would cost hundreds of
thousands even where obtainable. But this idea
of building companies of workmen, good as it was,
is no novelty to scores of men. Several attempts
had been made to establish co-operative building
companies, and a building company of working
men was in course of formation.

' Surprising progress has been made by the smiths

They started without a penny except what their

Special resolutions have been passed, authorising•

that. those wild stayed after' t} lock-out did so at

articles.title: CARPENTERS.
articles.text:
THE CARPENTERS.

The Committee of this branch of the building
trades have met every day duribg the week at the
Brown Bear, and the delegates have held two
meetings, at whieh a lot of routine business was
transacted.

Tlio Carpenter Central Committee, having re-
ceived the final returns of the number.of ear.
pouters Joeked Out, have struek the first week's
dividend. The returns are 1,000 .nion, ineiuding

240 men remaining on strike from the firms of
Messrs. Jackson and Shaw and Mr. Brass. The
dividend was struck at the rate of Is. 3d. per day
for each locked-out man, and Is. 9d. per day for
for each man on strike. This pay each man re-
ceived up to Friday night last.
The above dividend has been struck chiefly
from the money paid in from the levy laid upon
the carpenters in employment, no account of any
consequence having yet been received from other
trades or from the provinces. The society men
each receive 15s. per week from their respective,
societies, exclusive of the above--dividend. The
men were paid at the district committee-rooms on
Monday.

FRIDAY.—From enquiries made last night there
is no alteration in the aspect of affairs. The actual
position appears to be thus :—The masters consider
it useless to send any proposal to the men; and
the men, judging from the opinions expressed at
their meetings, are willing to receive and consider
any proposal from the master builders, but will
not accept any proposal coming from others. But
at the same time the men are not prepared to offer
any terms of compromise.

articles.title: MASONS.
articles.text:
THE MASONS.

The masons have mot every morning at the
Sun, Mason-street, Mr. Broadhurst in the chair.
The financial returns up to the present
time were considered very satisfactory, and the
first week's dividend would be given to
the men on Tuesday. A largo party of the locked-

being executed by a London firm. The railway
fares of these men
,had been paid, and they wore
to be paid London prices. In addition to this

at the open shops. The number or locked-out

of the foremen had acted upon tbe resolution

had come out; but sonic few (whose names were

at "fixing." These men could not be interfered

The chairman then addressed Alm :meeting,

articles.title: PLASTERERS.
articles.text:
THE PLASTERERS.

An aggregate meetieg of the men of the above
trade was held on Thursday night at the Agricul-
tural 11411. Mr. Maenamara in the chair.

The Chairman, on opening the proocedings,
said that all those present at`the meeting were no
doubt well aware that it had been convened for
the purpose of obtaining the nine hours at 9d, an
hour from the masters.

. The following resolution was proposed and

That the meeting do pledge itself to form a

The Chairman said that the question of 93. an

The third resolution was then put and carried-

That it is the opinion of the !retiring pro-

Mr. C. Williams, the secretary of the National

articles.title: SMITHS.
articles.text:
THE SMITHS.

In organisation, the smiths and rnetal-workers
are advancing. In accordance with the plan
agreed upon last week, they have opened four
local houses of call—one at the Harrison Arms, in
Gray's Inn-road ;Lie second at the King's 11(31)
Ebury Bridge; a third :at the Blenheim Arms,
Blenheim-street, Chelsea; and a fourth at the
Royal George, Westminster-road. Oa Friday
night a deputation was sent to the exeoutive of!
the Amalgamated Society of Engineers, to arrange
for obtaining regular support from that powerful '
body. The proposal made was promised immediate
consideration. Birmingham, being a large centre
of engineering labour, has been directly Com-
municated w:th. Letters from the smiths' com-
mittee were read at the engineers' lodges there on
Saturday night, audit response of some consequence
to the exchequer is anticipated. In London, and
not fur from the smiths' head-quarters in Soho, o
trade society of some standing has discovered
itself, and offered its services in promoting moro
general organisation. This body, which styles
itself the United Order of Smiths, has a number
of lodges in the metropolis, and a good many
branches in the country. Subscription sheets
have been forwarded to all branches.
A general committee of the smiths and metal
workers was held at the Rose and Crown in Soho,.
on Wednesday morning. The appeal to the trade
which had been drawn up at the end of last week
was finally considered and adopted. It advances
the nine hours as the only serious issue in the
strike, and refers as a good augury to the success
with which it has been fought out by other trades,,
notably by the Newcastle engineers. In a retro -
spect of the antecedents of the lock-out it appears
that the masters had had six months' notice before
the carpenters and joiners struck on the Ist Jlll3O.
The appeal is specially addressed to the iron
trades, and urges as a reason for its publication
the well-known circumstance of the carpenters'
committee having told the smiths they must loak
out for themselves. Mr. "William Allan, of the
Amalgamated Society of Engineers, 90, Black-
friars-road, will act as treasurer.

articles.title: LABOTTRERS.
articles.text:
THE LABOTTRERS.

A meeting, convened by the committee of the
locked-out building labourers, has been held in
Trafalgar-square, for the purpose of laying before
the public their present position. The Rev. G.
Murphy occupied the chair, and about %OW)
persons were present, chiefly of the working
and labouring class.

The Chairman) in opening the proceedings, said
he considered the building labourers who had been,
looked out were in every way deserving of the
support and sympathy of the public at large.,
They had not, like the skilled men in the building
trade, a society to fall back upon, and, as a rule,.
their low rate of wages when at work precluded
their saving anything. They had applied for
advice and assistance to the committee of the
masons and the carpenters, but they were informed,
that they had quite enough to do to help them-
selves. Therefore these poor men had no other,
resource but to throw themselves upon the
generosity of their more fortunate fellow-labourers
and a benevolent public.
Mr. Tuff moved the following resolution :
That in the opinion of this meeting the locked
-
out building labourers of London are deserving
of public support, inasmuch as they had not ie
any way aided in bringing about the present lock*
out.

Mr. Kenny seconded the resolution.
The resolution was unanimously adopted.
Mr. Halloran moved a resolution, pledging the
labourers preseut to join the newly-formal
society.
Mr. Mills seconded the resolution, which, 11%ving,_
been supported by several other labourers, iree
adopted.
The mating, which was most orderly, then
terminated, a !umber of the men remaining behind
to give in their names as members of the society-
.
to Mr. Halloran, the secretary.

_Juty 6, 1872.

On Saturday night the labourers at some of the
works in the metropolis also made collections.
Some unauthorized persons have gone about asking
for money under pretence of assisting the
labourers, and they wish it to be known that only
those having printed forms, dated from 51, Broad-
wall, signed by the treasurer and secretary, arc
entitled to make collections on their behalf. They
desire to thank those who have kindly sent them
intimation of need of labourers in certain localities,
but it will be still more valuable if employers
wanting labour would write direct to tbe central
committee, who sit daily at 51, Broadwall, S.E.,
stating rate of wages, the cheapest way for the men
to travel, and if any arrangement Would be made
to deduct the expenses by weekly instalments,
several of the men having wives and families,

whose industry brings them bread, and who want
to see their way before breaking up their homes.

articles.title: MASTER BUILDERS.
articles.text:
THE MASTER BUILDERS.

Mr. Bird, hon secretary of the Master Builders'
Central Association, has issued the following
statement :

"At a meeting of the committee of the Central
Association of Master Builders, held on Monday,
a communication was received from the Executive
Committee on Labour and Capital, appointed by
the Social Science Association, suggesting that a

court of arbitration should be at once constituted
consisting of an equal number of the represen-
tatives of employers and employed, who shall
at their first meeting elect an umpire or referee,
and that all matters in dispute shall be referred to
such court, whose decision shall be final, it being
agreed that pending such award both parties may
maintain their present position.
"The communication was signed by nine mem-
bers of Parliament, including Messrs. Mundella,
Cowper-Temple, T. Hughes, Auberon Herbert, and
others. After considerable discussion,the Committee
of the Central Association passed the following reso-
lution, and forwarded it at once to Mr. Peers, the
Secretary of the Social Science Association :

" • The Committee of the Central Assoeisition of
Master Builders aro willing to adopt the sugges-
tion made by the Committee on Labour and Capital
appointed by the Social Science Association, and
are quite ready to refer the pending questions to
a tribunal constituted as proposed and to abide by
its decision.'

"Up to this day the communication referred to

in some of the newspapers as having emanated
from the Trades Council, had not been received
by the Central Association of Master Builders.

"From the returns made to the Committee of
the Builder.' Association it appears that up to
the present time 85 firms have entirely locked out
and 65 more are under engagements to reduce the
men in their employ to the lowest possible number.
The firms referred to above comprise, with one or
two exceptions, all those of any importance who
supported the lock-out in 1859, and the groat
majority of those who have .risen to any position
since that time. The number of men locked out
does not equal tha number of men locked out in
1869, but is certainly more than double the largest
estimate put before the public by the workmen.
Upwards of 13,000 men are now either on strike or
locked out, and a groat portion of the difference
between this number and the number in 1859 is
accounted for by the continued depression in the
building trade of London, which has been the
main argument of the masters in resisting the do -
mands of the men.

" Communications have been receivekby the
Masters' Association of meetings which have been
called in the principal towns in the provinces for
co-operating with:the Masters of London, at which
measures will be taken for reducing the number
?f hands now contributing towards the strike.
/ "The rumours of want of faith on the part of
ROM of the London Masters in carrying out the
look-out, have been investigated by the Committee
of the Central Association, and have been found in
almost all cases to be either grossly exaggerated
or wholly untrue."

A long discussion ensued, in which the delegates
explained the position and feelings of their various
trades, and during which some misunderstandings
that had prevailed were satisfactorily cleared up.
The following resolution was ultimately adopted
"That in the opinion of this meeting, corn-
of delegates from the carpenters, masons,
plasterers, painters, smiths and metal workers, and
Libourers, it is desirable to form a central com-
mittee of deleptes of all trades affected by the
look-out, for the purpose of eo.lecting subscrip-
tions from the general trades, such subscriptions to
be divided equally among each trade in proportion
to the number of men locked out, but each trade
to have power to collect and appropriate the
levies and subscription from its own members, and
internally manage its ou n affairs."
It, was then resolved that the te)ove resolution
should be place,' before (a 0 tride for confirma-
tion, and the meeting stood adjourned until Monday
next.

articles.title: ACTION OF THE SOCIAL SCIENCE ASSOCIATION.
articles.text:
ACTION OF THE SOCIAL SCIENCE
ASSOCIATION.

At a meeting of the Executive Committee on
Labour and Capital, appointed by the Social
Science Association, held on Friday, it was re-
solved :

1. That the committee greatly regret that the
measures which were in progress for bringing the
present dispute between the master builders in
Lydon and their workmen to a friendly termina-
tion, by a meeting of the representatives of both
classes, and, if necessary,, by a reference to
arbitrators, have for the present failed.
2. That, as both parties to the present dispute
have expressed their approval of the principle of
arbitration, although neither party has succeeded
in submitting a definite proposal which the other
has thought it desirable to accept, the committee
venture to hope that, occupying as they do a per-
fectly neutral position; a suggestion on tlioir part
with a view to arbitration may meet with favour-
able consideration.

3. That the committee, therefore, respectfully
suggest a court of arbitration should 'be at once
constituted, consisting of an equal number of the
representatives of employers and employed, who
shall, at their first meeting, elect an umpire or
referee, and that all matters in dispute shall be
referred to such court, whose decisicn shall be
final, it being agreed that, pending such award,
both parties may maintain their present position.
The resolutions are signed by Mr. A. X.
ffundella, Mr. R. Torrens, Mr. W. Cowper
Temple, Mr. Thomas Hughes, Mr. Samuel Morley,_
Mr. W. Morrison, Mr. Anberon Herbert, Mr.'
George Dixon, and Mr. Thomas Brassey.

articles.title: CONFERENCE OF THE BUILDING
articles.text:
CONFERENCE OF THE BUILDING

TRADES.

On Monday afternoon a conference of represen-
tatives from the various branches of the building
trade, convened by the Carpenters' Committee,
was held at the Brown Bear, Bloomsbury, for the
purpose of considering the propriety of establish-
ing a central committee for conducting the move-
ment, and making a united appeal to the general
trades for support. The following delegates were
attendance :—Masons, Messrs. liroddhurst and
Barrett; carpenters, Messrs. Davis and Barry.;
plasterers, Messrs. Westoby and Sainsbury ;
painters, Messrs. G. Shipman and Gahagan ;
smiths ,and metal workers, Messrs. Baker and
Wells; labourers, Messrs. Bresnahan and Kenny.
Mr. ' Shipton was elected as chairman, and Mr.
Matkin, of the Carpenters' Committee, as secre-
tary. A letter was read from the Bricklayer's
Committee, stating that they had no power to
send delegates ußtil after they had consulted
their executive council.

The Chairman opened the proceedings by ex-
plaining the °Neat of the meeting. A central com-
mittee would certainly prevent much confusion,
would give more satisfaction and confidence to the
general trades, and be more in the intere'st of the
trades locked-out, as they could thus show a
united front to the employers.

articles.title: LONDON DOCK LABOURERS.
articles.text:
THE LONDON DOCK LABOURERS.

A numerously attended meeting took place on
Monday night at Stepney-green, to take into
consideration the condition of the dock and wharf
.labourers in London, more especially those in
connection with the East India Docks, now on
'strike. An appeal on the part of the men alluded
to Am an advance of pay having failed to meet
with a favourable response. from the , Dock
Company, they resolved at the close of last
.Monday's work "not to go in," and subsequently:
an application to Mr. Ellwood, hon. secretary to
,the Labour. Protection League, for advice in the
matter, induced that gentleman to take an active
part in the proceedings on Monday. A temporary,
'platform was erected in trout of the Mulberry
Tree Inn, and in opening the meeting Mr. Ellwood
alluded to the • ill-paid and half-starved condition
of the men, for whose protection, and that of their
wives and families, they bad assembled, lie
could not but censure the men for having taken
the step they had without at first soliciting the
aid of those competent to judge; and lo advised
them not to resort to any, thoughtless acts, but to
pursue their course wisely and judiciously, and.
they would ultimately be enabled to demand a
fair day's pay for 'a fair day's labour. He further
proposed that the men should form themselves
into branches in connection with the League,
which suggestion was favonrably received, and
eventually the only resolution submitted was
proposed by a Mr. Senior, and seconded by a Mr.
Chapman, both labourers, It was as follows :
" That this meeting is of opinion that they do
not go into work under the minimum pay of 6d.
per hour for all grades of labour." The. recopticn
of the resolution was unanimous, the cheering
lasting for at least five minutes; after whioa Mr.
Roberts, a timber merchant, we understood, made
a telling speech, sympathising till poor
labourers in every particular.

articles.title: AMALGAMATED SOCIETY 0 F LONDON TAILORS.
articles.text:
THE AMALGAMATED SOCIETY 0 F
LONDON TAILORS.

An association taa above wal formed on Sunday
evening last, at a numerously-attended meeting
hold in the Minories. Hitherto it would seem that
the working tailors of the East have not been
united and organized for the purpose of augment-
ing their wages and generally bettering their oon-
dition as a trade. They have, it is true, a sort of
benefit or friendly society, which affords Telief in
eases of sickness distress, &c., but unlike other
branches of industry, they wanted the combina-
tion and machinery requisite to bring such:pressure
upon their employers as would mull) for them
more
„pay and reduced hours of labour. To sup-
ply this want "The Amalgamated Society of
London Tailors" has been instituted, and the
heartiness and unanimity which characterised the
proceedings on Sunday augurs well for its success.
The tailors—who, from what we can learn, appear
to be as ill paid and hard-worked a body of men as
any in or out of the metropolis—start their move-
ment with a distinct avowal that they do not wish to
strike, and they express a hope that their employers
will see the reasonableness of their requirements
and accede to them without recourse being had to
strong measures. Although the association has
been initiated by men who for the most part
belong to
,the Jewish persuasion, tailors of all
shades of religious belief are invited to become
members. The question is not one of race or reli-
gion at all, but, as the members put it, one of
humanity, justice, and reason. An excellent branch
was formed.

articles.title: STRIKE OF THAMES LIGHTER-
articles.text:
STRIKE OF THAMES LIGHTER-

MEN.

On Tuesday a numerously-atteni ed meeting of
master-lightermen and barge•owners was held at
St. Dunstan's-house, Cross-lane, Lower Thames
street, to consider the demand of the working
lightcrmen for an increase of wages. 15tr. W. S.
Page was called to the chair.

Amongst those present wero Messrs. Phillipps,
Graves, PhiHipps, and Co.; G. 'Ward and Sons;
W. A. Joyee and- Sons; Bells and Taylor; J.
Stuchbury and Sons; • Thorn, Hart, and. Co.;
Dicey and Puzey ; Pillow, Jones, and Co.;
Middlemist and Sons ;. Lamb, Key, and Dards ;
_

Page, Son, and Emit; Newcombe and Thomson;
J. W. Turnley ; Wilkinson - and Dawson; H.
Grey, jun. ; Mercantile .Lighterage Company; E.
Hough and Co.,' and many others. It may be
stated that a number of lightermen employel
on the Thames have made a demand for an
increase of wages, with an intimation that unless
an advance. ',was granted they 'would cease
work on Friday Week. This has caused
much excitement, - not only in the trade,
but amongst Merchants and largo shippers, and a'.
desire was generally expressed to meet the men in
a fair spirit. It was contended, hoWever, that the
demand of the men was unreasonable, and could
not be complied with. It was urged that what-
ever grounds the men might have for an increase
of pay, it could not be said that their wages were
anything like unreasonably low, considering their
position and the character of their employment, or.
that they were overworked. It was denied that
the masters had declined to confer with the men;
indeed the employers &sired to meet them, and to
discuss the matters in dispute with them. It was
also 'remarked that the men were seldom kept 'at
actual work more than five or six Aura a 'clay, the
rest of their time being occupied in waiting for

the tides to take craft in and out of dock. It was
also observed that while the men receive pay for
being detained alongside a ship, the employer had
no compensation for the detention of his craft.
After some dis'cussioa it was arranged that a com-
mittee should be appointed to con'aider the question
of-wages, and to meet a deputation of the men on
the subject. A committee was selected, and
it was agreed to hold a meeting at Waterman's

Hall on Thursday afternoon, and that one man
from each firm thas had received notice should be
invited to attend:

A large meeting of lighterraen was held at the
Edinburgh Cagle, Mile End, on Sunday night, to
consider grievances under which the men labour.
The chair was taken by Mr. Elliot, a lighterman.
It was stated that a union had been formed for
the protection of their common interests. A
memorial had been drawn up and signed by nearli
all the lighteruaen of London, requesting that
their working day might be reduced to twelve
hours instead of eighteen hours, as at present,
and also requesting 6s. a day and 63. for each
night woiked. If the masters refuse to grant the
request of this
.memorial, the men have agreed to
strike at the end of this week. A deplorable
picture was drawn by some of the speakers of the
hardships and discomforts which lightermen have
to endure.

articles.title: LONDON WAREHOUSEMEN.
articles.text:
THE LONDON WAREHOUSEMEN.

On Sunday night a crowded meeting of porters,
packers, and warehousemen, chiefly connected
with City firms, was held at the Red Lion
Tavern, Red Lion-court, Fleet-street, to consider
the present rate of wages and the hours of work-
ing.

The ohair was taken by a foreman packer, who
stated that the .objet of the meeting was to form
a complete organization amongst themselves.
. A Warehouseman, after stating that it was im-
possible for the men to meet except on Sunday,
said that they could not do better than form the
Porters, Packers, and Warehousemen's Protection
Society. Tie might remark, that, because ho had
distributed the circulars calling this meeting, ho
had been dismissed from his' employment on
saturday. (Cries of "Shame.") .
In the course of a discussion which followed,
a packer told the meeting that after twelve years':
service he got 235. a week. When he asked fey
an advance his master told him he could not
give it, as he had just altered his premises.'
A. City packer said he knew many houses
where the men worked until two o'clock in the

articles.title: morning.
articles.text:
morning.

The Chairman raid he knew a man who had.
been tvrenty-two years in one house and got 224.1
a week. When he asked for an increase, and said
he had a very large family, the City magnate re
fused, and added that it was unfortunate the man.,
had so large a family.,
A porter suggested that work after seven o'clock
ought to be paid for extra.

The Chairman spoke of a large house in Cannon.:
street where the men got only £l3 a year, with
board and lodging. That was less than the soldier
got, and the men worked every day all the year
round, Saturdays included.

A Warehouseman: Policemen are gentlemen to
us. They get 10a. and 21s. a week and their
clothes. They labour by walking, but we do hard.
bodily work.

A City warehouseman said he had to be at work
at seven a.m., and if he was a few minutes late he
had to do an extra week's work "on the gas"
(which means looking after the lighting and.
extinguishing the lights in the warehouse). 1-10.
got 21s. a week, and had to work seventeen hours
out of the twenty-four throe months in the year,
and generally thirteen hours the rest of the year.

A City packer said the slaves of the Southern
States used to be treated mildly compared with the
way in which the:porters and packers of the City
were treated In the btisy season he worked, like
his fellows, from seven a.m. to ' two the next
morning. These men in the -City had the wealth

LONDON DISTRICT BRANCH OF THE
GENERAL POST OFFICE.
To the Right Honourable W. Mouse% 11. P.,
Her Majesty's Postmaster General.
The petition of the sorters attached to the
East Central District Office of the G.P.O.

• Sheweth,---That we respectfully solicit an im-
mediate increase in our wages to the aulouut of
three shillings; per week, and that an annual
increment of two shillings per week be granted us
4ntil the maximum amount of our pay be
arrived at.

We also respeotfully submit to your notice the
arduous duties we are called upon to perform, and
to call your attention to the increased and still
increasing price of house rent, tales, and also of
provisions generally, and which at our present
rate of wages, we are unable to command.

Should you grant this, the prayer of your
memorialists, your petitioners will ever pray, &e.
Presented four months ago; not granted yet.

The General Post-Office is a peculiar institution.
It is the only Government department which
returns a profit; it has annexed its natural oppon-
ent, the telegraph system, and it has diversified
its duties by opening a Savings Bank; it is noted
for originating schemes about postal districts,
halfpenny postage, and postal cards, which,
excellent as they are in theory, are strangled in
practice by official red-tape. It occasionally dis-
tinguishes itself by liberal concessions, which,
like the reduction of the charges for money-
orders, are considerably more apparent than real.
Nevertheless, though we all grumble at it,
we all in the end put up with it, and 'when our
complaints about lost letters simply produce a
printed form from St. Martin's-le-grand, and two
or three calls from polite officers, who point out that
the letters cannot have been lost, we submit
to the illu4on with the best possible grace.
Let us hope that our sufferance will not lead
the Department to disregard a very weighty ob.
jection to a system which bids fair to be a national
disaster if it be persisted in. When we read
advertisements headed "Post Office," and learn
that situations are offered for boys from 15 to 17
years of age, and that candidates may attend at
the Civil Service. Commission, Cannon-row, West
minster, the announcement at first sight looks
like a fair and proper extension of the system of
open competition. Unfortunately this is only the
first appearanee of these lads of 15 and 17 in
print. The final record of too many will be found
elsewhere. Since the Post Office began to employ
these lads there has been an increase of Post
Office cases at the Central Criminal Court, and
the printed raturns show that the increase
is due to the number of youths of 15
and 17 who are charged with offences by
the Postmaster General. These young fellows,
at the very outset of their career, are branded as
criminals, and sentenced to punishments varying
from five years' penal servitude to three days'
imprisonment. We do not say that such punish-
'vents may not be deserved. Those who succunib
to temptation must suffer; but woe be to those
who offer the temptation. Reading ;and writing
' are the sole qualifications examined into in Cannon-
row ere these mere b.oys are appointed to positions
,of strong temptation, of a responsibility o
whose gravity they have no conception. Lads
from industrial schools, orphans who have not
known the moral influence of a mother or father,
boys who, if placed in situations suited for a boy,
would have arrived at years of discretion with
good characters, fall victims, te tbe Post Office
passion for cheap labour. It would seem as if it
were easier to dete3t the erring lad with a test-
letter end to persecute him at the Old Bailey than
it ia to incoira into his training and fitness for a
responsible employment. The sessions for the last
three months seem to point to this conclusion, for
at each a lad has been tried for Post Offixe
robbery; though in one instance, we believe, the
offence was rather the delay than the theft of
letters. '

• Such a atette of things cannot be permitted to
continue. Economy must not be exercised till it

hecotaes acius.e arid' we trtiat that the aubjeet
will be taken up in Parliament. A profitable de-
partment must not be the means of blasting the
career of poor lads, tried beyond their strength,'
when their moral as their physical development is
not "set." Boys for boys' work, and men for
men's work, must be the rule at St. Martin's-le-
Grand; and then, to the delight of all right-
thinking men, will disappear, thank God, from the
felons' dock at the 01d Bailey that pale cowering
lad of fifteen or seventeen, who has, for the last
year or so, too often stood there to plead to "a
Post Office offence."— Weekly :Dispatch,: June: 30,
1872.

ia the service; by publishing the [present rate

In conclusion, he said, the society would watch

THE STRIKE AND 'LOCK-OUT IN TUB

BUILDING T RADIM

--*-^
THERE is, no doubt, a strong desire in the
public mind that the strike and look-out in
the building trades should find an amioable
settlement. In fact, from all quarters where
any right to snake a suggestion can "'lst'
there is heard expressed the desire that this
unfortunate quarrel should be settled by
reason and at once, and not by force, and after
prolonged loss and suffering have come to
those engaged in it.

• The suggestion of the Trades Council hag
not been favourably received by the men, a, ,na'
we cannot see that, even if the men accartea,
it, the employers would adopt it. It is not 1
we think, likely that the nine hours would be
conceded, and only the other two propositioni
left to be arbitrated on, but it may be said in
its favour that it is better than the proposal
of the men themselves, which withdrew the
two most important questions, leaving only
the third to be decided by arbitration.
To us it appears that arbitration ought to
include everything. To rely on it as a
principle to be useful in ad times and seasonis

it should be acted on without reservation.
What substantial good could possibly be ex-
pected, if, whenever a misunderstanding
arose, employers or working men, instead of
putting their whole ease, insisted upon with-
drawing such parts of it as either might feel
determined to have settled in their own way
and in no other. We ask what the men and
their friends would have said if the employers
had taken precisely the stand taken by the
men, and insisted that the nine hours and the
extra pay should be given up, and the work-
ing rules only put before the tribunal called
on to arbitrate. Such a proceeding, what-
ever side it may come from, is inconsistent
and meaningless, and cannot therefore meet
with the approval of fairminded men. The
proposal of the Trades Council on this ground
alone—even though it only withdraws one of
the questions in dispute instead of two,
should be held as inadmissible, seeing that
anything which limits the legitimate action
of a board of arbitrators destroys the value on
the principle on whioli it acts.
The proposition of the Social Science Com-
mittee is much better, because it proposed to
arbitrate the whole queslion. But it errs in
asking for a perfected tribunal at once. Its
proposal as to the mode of constituting a board
may be the best that can be made, but this is
not the momentito set aboutsuch a work. What
is required just now is not a board formed with
a view to permanence and continuous action,
but rather two or three men appointed to deal
with the ease at once, and who, by being so
appointed, would be more likely to carry
the confidence of those who named them to the
settlement of the dispute. The formation of a
regular board should be an afterwork, deli-
berately and carefully undertaken and exe-
cuted.

Mr. FREDERICK SAGE'S letter in the Daily
News is everything that could be desired in
spirit, but his plan would not work without
modification. To make the decisions of
arbitrators binding for" ten years," in a labour
market fluctuating like ours,:would be to make
them practically inoperative. A time, how-
ever, might be fixed, to which all would agree,
and then we have no doubt it would
work very well, The right thing to do
now is for the employers and the
workmen to get together at ono by some
kind of mutual representation, and settle the
questions in dispute on a fair and reasonable
basis. Mr. MAUL; in the Builders' Trade
Circular, advises a general lock-out through-
out the provinces. . We do not think such a
thing can take place ; but if it should we
cannot imagine anything more savage, more
gratuitously cruel than such a proceeding; and
if anything was required to show bow brutal
men may become when engaged in warfare, on
behalf of their interests, this detestable sugges-
tion would furnish it.

articles.title: WAY THE MONEY GOES.
articles.text:
THE WAY THE MONEY GOES.

Tux British artisan is quite as alive to the
beauties of art as any other man. But there
are, or ought to be, limits to everything; and,
in works of art, the public are entitled to
claim money's worth; all the more because in
such bargains the money slips away by large
handfuls. The lobbies of the louses of
Parliament are what is styled "adorned' with
paintings in fresco. Now, if pictures of that
kind have any recommendation above pictures
painted in the ordinary way, it is that they
are supposed to be everlasting. Already,
however, are the frescoes in the Palace of our
Legislature fast crumbling away. What, we
wonder, would be said of a common plasterer
if the inner walls made by him came to dust
in this manner? We have not before us at
this moment the whole cost fruitlessly incurred
for these everlasting paintings that have no
durability in them. From a few specimens,
however, we may judge of the whole, as to the
rate at which the people's money has been
fooled away. Two of these worthless works,
for example, were done by the late Mr.
IficusE, an artist of undoubted merit; yet,
what signifies that, if the man's work dies
almost as soon as the man himself? "The
Death of Nimsolf," and "the Meeting of
WELLINGTON and BLIICILER" were done by this
master, and cost the immense sum of £7,500
each. "Let any one look at them now," says
Mr. BERIT.u, OssoRNE, " those pictures which

were to have lasted for ever. BLIICICER is
almost obliterated, and the famous nose of the
Duke of WELLINoToN has dropped off his face.
In short, every fresco in the House is rotting
off the walls."

It was a great pity the gentlemen facetiously
termed "masters" had not made themselves
masters of the art before they went meddling
and muddling in this fashion at the tax-
payers' expense. Instead of this, they took
the money, and gave us in return what, under
the promise of being beautiful for ever, has
proved as evanescent as the morning cloud
or the early dew which soon vanishes away.
Now that the money has been thrown away,
they and those who employed them are be-
ginning to inquire what could have been the
secret of permanency in the paintings. of this
description upon ancient walls; and, so far as
we can see, Minister, artist, and chemist, are
as much in the dark on the subject as the
artistes were at the beginning of the foolish
and wasteful experiment.

The worst of it is, that the fresco fiasco does
not restrain those who have the mismanage-
ment of such things from plunging with equal
ignorance and uncertainty into new experi-
ments. It was determined by the Royal Com-
mission, that the four patron saints, ST.
GEORGE, ST. DAVID, ST. ANDREW, and Sr.
PATRICK, should be illustrated in the four
compartments of the Central Hall. Sr. GEORGE
and the Dragon have been done, not in
fresco, but in Venetian mosaic, which is
composed of glass. The question is now,
whether the brother saints shall be done in
the same manner, or all the four in what Mr.
OSBORNE, who is a cognoscente, stigmatises as
"abominable fresco." On the comparative
merits of the two methods, those Members who
pretend to know all about it are so entirely
at odds, that, as Alderman Lusx told them, it
was quite impossible for a plain man to under-
stand what they really wanted. All that we can
make out in this tangle of talk is, that, having
ridiculously failed in the attempt to revive
a lost art, some of them are disposed to betake
themselves to one confessedly so novel as to
be still in the first stage of its development!
The painters themselves pronounce against
the glass and for the fresco, alleging that, at
last, a chemist has turned up who knows all
about it, and who will show them how to re-
store the art in all its perfection. The
painters naturally take their own side, but
other people would like to have some proof
that the man of science whom they have
hunted up has really discovered the principle
of fixing the colours in the substance of the
wall, before embarking further in this cosily
order of dissolving views. On th is point, ire,
Member for Waterford put opinion in the
House to the test, by moving to strike out the
item of £5OO for painting one panel of the four
in the Central Hall in fresco, by way of com-
parison with the ST. GEORGE and the DRAGON
in Venetian mosaic. The House so much
agreed with him that the item was struck out
without a division. As the painters condemn
the glass and Parliament the frescoes, Mr.
AYRTON is placed in as great a fix as Mr.
Alderman Lusx ; but a chock has been
given to foolish and wasteful experiments.

THE AGRICULTURAL LABOURERS OF

SOMERSETSIIIRE.

Trrz movement for the improvement of the
condition of the agricultural labourers is pro-
gressing favourably in all parts of the country,
as will be seen from the reports which we have
published during the last few weeks; and the
labourers have only to be firm, patient, and
determined a little longer, for the time of their
redemption draweth nigh._

In gomersetshire, the labourers' case is per-
haps the worst of any, and their condition is
certainly one of deep degradation. But it is
worthy of observation that a good friend has
come to their assistance in the person of Mr.
GronoE MlTemzu,, of London, formerly a farm
labourer at Montaeute. Mr. MITCUELL'S sym-
pathy with the depressed labourers of his na-
tive county has induced him to hold a series
of meetings, at which the labourers have
attended in large numbers, and enrolled
themselves as members of the Union.

The meetings that have ahead; been held
prove the usefulness of giving the labourers

the opportunity of telling their own grievances,
in the presence of impartial friends, from a
public platform in the open air. The meetings
at Montacute and Chard have been the means
of calling the attention of the people of
Somersetshire to the question, and these we
understand are to be followed up by holding
meetings at Bridport and Crewkorne.

attend these meetings, and state the labourers'

THE MINES REGULATION BILL.

ANOTHER, but unsuccessful attempt, has
been made to mutilate and effectually emas-
culate the Mines Regulation Bill. After an
unsatisfactory conversation on the subject of
inspection, several clauses passed, until the
House in Committee came to that providing
general rules for working and ventilation.
Mr. Evuorr proposed to amend the sub-
section; namely—" That an adequate amount
of ventilation shall be constantly produced in
every mine to dilute and render harmless
noxious gases to such an extent that the
working places of the shafts, levels, and
working of such mines, and the travelling
roads to and from such places, shall b 3 in a
fit state for working and passing therein."
His amendment was to insert after the word
"shall," in the latter part, the words, "under
ordinary circumstances." He stated that, on
extraordinary occasions, he had known enor -
mous quantities of gas to escape per minute,
which no amount of ventilation would dilute.

In fact, ventilation would be dangerous, be-
cause gas, when not mixed with atmospheric
air, was inexplosive, but, when diluted, was
highly combustible. He therefore hoped the
right honourable gentleman would not oppose
his amendment nor even venture upon a reply.
Mr. BRUCE did not yield to this rather
singular demand. But he allowed Mr.
Foruzuoin to speak first. For seven years,
said that gentleman, he had had no accident
in his mines, although he had raised over six
million tons of coals, but ho always trembled
lest some tremendous explosion should ensue.

It was not a gradual precolation, which they
might combat by efficient ventilation, but
there occurred vast accumulation of gas,
which, when freed by perhaps a stroke of the
pick, filled the whole mine. It was utterly
impossible to provide against such contin-
gencies, and a perfect delusion to rely on the
safety lamp alone. The only thing a minor
could do when he struck into a blower and

liberated the gas, was to report to the manager,
who would take the precautions necessary.
He did not think, therefore, there was any
justification for this penal legislation.
ThellOILE SECRETARY, in answer to these re-
presentations, referred to the foots of former
inquiry. In 1865 a Committee of experienced
members agreed almost without exception
to many recommendations. One agreed to
without a division was, "Your Committee
have recommended the omission of the words
'under ordinary circumstances' in the
first rule, on the ground that there might be
circumstances which, though not strictly
ordinary, were such as might have been
foreseen and guarded against; but your Com-
mittee recommend that the owners and
managers of mines should be entitled to plead
as a sufficient defence in proceedings against
them, that they had taken all reasonable
precautions." On that recommendation the
present clauqe was founded. He agreed that
great difficulties acose from the miners
suddenly ooming upon great quantities of gas,
but that gas did not become explosive until
mixed with four times its bulk of common
air, and became quite harmless when mixed
with fourteen times its bulk; so that, after all,
it was a mere question of efficient ventilation.
It would be for the owner to show all reason-
able precaution. The country had called

aloud upon the Government to prevent, if
possible, deplorable accidents, and the only
way was to increase the responsibility of the
owners. If all mines were managed like
those of the members for Glamorganshire,
North Durham, and Merthyr, there would be
no necessity for legislation; but, in the latter
case, it was quite notorious the mines were in
a fiery district. He had been charged with
too much warmth. He felt warmly. IL
seemed to him that, this being a Bill for the
protection of miners, the Government were
betrayed when the House admitted an amend-
ment destroying that protection by making it
impossible to prove that children had been
employed before the proper time. He had
been told by those who stood between masters
and men that, if Government would withdraw
their support of the general rules as they
stood in the Bill, the masters would concede
the question of payment by weight instead of
measure. If that was true, it must have the
most discouraging effect upon those who wished
to serve the men. He voted for payment by
weight; but, whether it was in the Bill or not
was of little importance; because not neces-
sarily connected with safety,' whereas the
Government looked upon this clause as all-
important.

Having, on former occasions, been some-
what severe upon the langour of Mr. BirucE,
'we are bound to applaud his present steadfast-
ness and vigour. After a second fire of
coal-owners, however, he authorised the
ATTORNEY•GENERAL, in his name, to concede
the qualifying words "so far as possible," in
the provision requiring the owner to keep the
mine in a fit state for working and passing.
At this point, Dr. PLAYFAIR came to the side
of the miners. If" practicable" were substi-
tuted for "possible," it would meet the case;
but he totally objected to the words "under
ordinary circumstances." A paper had been
lately road before the Royal Society which
indicated, in his judgment, conclusively, that
71 per cent, of the explosions in 1868, 1869,
and 1870 were duo to barometrical depressions
and risings, and he did not see why the mine-.
owner should not be made as responsible for
non-attention to those changes as the captain
of a ship. To the first suggestion of the
learned member, Mr. BRUCE acceded, but
firmly resisted Mr. ELLIOT'S pleasure, and the
amendment was lost on a division by 298
against 20. This overwhelming majority is
the first expression of the anxiety of Mr.
DrsutEra. and his party for the health and
safety of the people.

articles.title: WEEK'S NEWS.
articles.text:
THE WEEK'S NEWS.

On Saturday evening the annual dinner of
the Commercial Travellers' Benevolent Insti-
tution took place at St. James's Hall, the
Lord Mayor presiding. The donations an-
nounced (luting the evening amounted to about
X5OO.

Sir W. Stephenson, ohairman of the Board
of Inland Revenue, has acted upon the sug-
gestion of the Chancellor of the Exchequer
with regard to the regulation of Working
Men's Clubs. In future, shoulds clubs selling
excisable liquors deposit a copy of their rules
with the Board, and adhere to them if ap-
proved by that body, those institutions will be
quite secure from prosecution.

The Revenue Returns for the quarter as well
as for the year ending the 30th June,
,have
been issued. During the past three months
the national income has amounted to
£18,393,507, a net increase of rather more
than a million and. a half over the receipts in
the corresponding period of last year. The
revenue for the year has been £76,260,038,
and this was a net increase of £5,793,629 over
that of the twelve mouths ending June 30,
1871. The chief cause of this augmentation
was the income tax, which yielded more by
£3,494,000.

A. dock labourer on strike, who had been
guilty of the offence of intimidation, was on.
Saturday sentenced to a month's imprison-
ment with hard labour by the Thames Police
magistrate.

In the French Assembly on Saturday, the
Bill imposing a tax of three per cent. on stooks
and shares was passed after some discussion.
The tax applies to foreign as well as French
securities. •

A. motion of M. Coquerel in the French
Protestant Synod, proposing that pastors
should be appointed by universal suffrage,
was rejected on Saturday, and it was decided
that they should be nominated by Presby-
terian Councils,

A. decree has been issued dissolving the
Spanish Cortes, and fixing the elections for
the 24th of August. The new Parliament is
to open on thd 15th of September.

According, to a Madrid telegram, the Car-
list movement is now ap completely at an end
that no band of more than twenty-five men is
anywhere to be met with.

Though a fortnight will elapse before the
text sitting of the Tribunal at Geneva, there
is still much to be done in the interim. In
all probability, the Court, when dealing with
the Direct Claims, will consider separately the
character of the Confederate cruisers, and
award damages according as they judge
England responsible for their depredations.
Should the amount named in gross be some-
where near the contending estimates, the matter
willbe settled; otherwise, the award of damages
will be referred to the assessors provided for
under the Treaty. The Berlin Arbitration on
the San Juan question will now proceed.
Prince Dismal.* will appoint eminent inter-
national jurists to examine the papers and
report to the Emperor.

An inquest was held on Saturday on the body
of Sarah Anne Rogers, who is alleged to have
died from injuries inflicted by her husband,
a barber in Bermondsey. A verdict of" Wilful
murder" against him was returned.

Another tragedy was perpetrated in Ber-
rnondsey on Sunday, when a dealer in old
metals, named William Edward Taylor, 89
years of age, brained to death a woman who
Lad lived with him. He at the some time
killed their little girl, five years of age. Taylor
afterwards attempted to commit suicide.

On Saturday evening the negotiations
between France and Germany were brought to
a conclusion, and the Treaty for the more
sredy evacuation of French territory was
signed at Versailles by M. de Remuso.t and
Count Arnim.

At the annual meeting of the Society for the
Suppression of Vice, NN Ina was held on Mon-
day, attention was drawn to the unremitting
exertions of this organization to check the
sale of improper literature, and hopes were
expressed that the result of the year's trans-
actions would convince the most sceptical of
the gravity and extent of the evil to be sup-
pressed.

Dr. Renard's release has been definitely
agreed to by the Government at Madrid; and
Saturday's Gazette captained the degree for-
mally dissolving the Corte and Congrese. The
elections are fixed for the 24th of August, and
the meeting of the Cortes will take place on
the 15th of September. Probably as indicating
0, change of policy in Cuba, the Spanish
Government has appointed a now Captain
(teneral of the island.

The Bethnal-green Museum was last week
visited by :50,883 persons. During the SaTllO
time the number of visitors to the South Ken-
sington Museum was 16,975.

A public meeting, characterised by scenes
of considerable animation, was held on Mon-
day afternoon at St. James's-hall, to protest
against the provisions in the Government
Licensing Bill, relating to the hours of closing
in the metropolis. Mr. Straight, M.P., pre-
sided. The opposition to the proposed change
was led by Mr. J. B. Buckstone, whose expe-
rience, as lessee of the Haymarket, satisfied
him that no alteration was needed. A resolu-
tion in favour of the existing system was met
by an amendment expressing approval of the
shorter hours as proposed in the Government
measure, but the former was carried—a result
which was followed by a free fight in the body
of the hall.

Mr. Arnold, at Westminster, was asked to
decide a case under the Act by which the pro-
perty of convicted felons, instead of being
forfeited to the Crown, may be realised by
persons properly appointed for the benefit of the
family. A. man who had attempted to murder
his wife was sentenced to penal servitude for
five years, and the wife made application to
dispose of his business for £4O, so as to pay off
a bill of sale of £24, and do something for
herself and family. &me guarantee was re-
quired by the intending purchaser as to her
power to sell, and the magistrate complied
with her request, appointing her brother ad-
ministrator to the convict's estate.

There is much activity upon Wimbledon-
common, where some of the competing corps
have already taken up their positions in
readiness for the National Volunteer Prize
Meeting, which begins on Monday next.

The National Memorial to the Prince Con-
sort, erected in Hyde-park, was on Monday
visited by the Queen, the Duke of Edinburgh,
Princess Louise, the Princess Beatrice, and
Prince Leopold. The proceedings were entirely
devoid of ceremonial, and very few persons
witnessed her Majesty's arrival or departure.
The monument was subsequently visited by a
considerable number of persons invited by the
Executive Committee.

Mr. Russell Gurney, M.P., was on Monday
present at a Foresters.' dinner at Southampton,
this being the first occasion on which he had
publicly met his constituents since his return
from Washington. The right hon, gentleman
gave some interesting details of his experiences
of the American people during his sojourn
amongst them, speaking in high terms of the
cordiality of his reception. He also took oc-
casion to correct,, an impression that the people
of the United States regarded this country
with hostile feelings. It was true that they
had felt hurt at some of the hard expressions
used. iere in reference to the preparation of the
American" Case," but of the ultimate beneficial
result of the Treaty of, Washington he had no
(loubt whatever.

At the Clerkonwoll Police-court on Monday
John Horuibrook, who had been in custody on
suspicion of having caused the death of his
mother, was discharged in consequence of the
insufficiency of the evidence in support of the
ac ou ation against him.

Henry Taylor, described as a sham doctor of
philosophy, was on Monday charged at Marl-
borough-street with baying attempted to de-
fraud Mr. Julian Ooldstnid, M.P. He was
remanded.

A fatal explosion took place on Monday at
a cartridge manufactory at Witton, near Bir-
mingham. The manager was killed, and
several other persons were injured.

Another of the suits by which in Equity the
Claimant to the Doughty estates is prosecuting
his claims was heard before Vice-Chancellor
Sir J. Wickens. An order had already been
made on the application of some of the defen-
dants, dismissing the bill unless proceedings
were taken within five weeks. A similar
order was now made on behalf of the other
defendants, and the time for prosecuting the
suit limited to a month.

Advice was asked of the Master of the Rolls
by the trustees under a settlement, whether
they would be justified in advancing a sum of
money to Frederick Ward, a lieutenant in the
army, one of the children of the marriage to
which the settlement referred; such stun
having been left specially for the purchase of
promotion, and purchase being now abolished.
Lord Romilly could not advise the trustees to
accede to the request, under the circumstances
named, but gave leave of appeal to the Lords
Justices.

Mr. Barker, the magistrate, at Clerkenwell,
while in the act of complaining bitterly of the
noise of a cock near the Court, was inter-
rupted by a defiant crow, and sent a policeman
out in plain clothes to arrest the offending
bird, but without suoooss.

Two Cambridge under-graduates " down "
for the Long Vacation were summoned before
the Brentford magistrates on Saturday, and
tined 403. each, for wantonly knocking down
an old gentleman in the street, at Ealing, on
the evening of the 24th of June, causing in-
juries from which he remained unconscious
until eleven o'clock the following morning.
The defence set up was that the defendants
had been at a cricket match, and were in a
hurry to catch the train.

• M. Engelhard, the Radical Prefect of the
Maine and Loire during the Ministry of M.
Gambetta, has been sentenced at Orleans to
500 francs fine, and 3,000 francs damages, for
publicly defaming, during his administration,
two Conservative gentlemen in that depart-
ment.

At an inquest held at Ipswich last week, on
the body of a youth who had been accidentally
drowned while bathing in the river Orwell,
Ur. George Sampson Elliston, a surgeon of
that town, stated in the course of his evidence,
"There are so many valuable rules and sug-
gestions in the printed regulations issued by
the Royal National Lifeboat Institution (In-
struction for Restoring the Apparently
Drowned), that I think they ought to be more
generally distributed and known along the
banks of the river." It may be mentioned
that the National Lifeboat Institution is pre-
pared to supply, on application, copies of these
valuable rules to coroners and other officers
throughout the United Kingdom. They are
based on the principles of the late distinguished
physiologist, Dr. Marshal flail, combined with
those of Dr. 11. It. Silvester, and are the result
of extensive inquiries made by the Institution
about seven years ago amongst medical men
and medical bodies, both at home and on the
Continent. These instructions have been cir-
culated throughout the United Kingdom and
in the colonies. They are also in use in her
Majesty's fleet, in the Coast Guard Service,
and at all the stations of the British Army at
home and abroad.

The death is announced of M. Michel Carre,
aged fifty-six, a well-known writer for the
French stage, and author of the libretti of
many of the most successful operas of the
last twenty years. Among others may be
mentioned the "Nowa de Jeannette," tho "Par-
don de Ploormel," "Lalla Itoukb," "Mignon,"
&e.

--- -
The 15th annual report of the trustees of the
National Portrait Gallery, contains a list of
several additional contributions of pictures
during the past year. Many important pur-
chases have also been made,including a portrait
of William •Pulteney, Earl of Bath, 1682-
1764, painted by Sir Joshua Reynolds.
Amongst the donations is a meeting of the
Royal Commission of Fine Arts at G wydyr-
house in the year 1846, painted by John
Partridge, and presented by the artist in
March last. Of tho twenty-eight noblemen
and gentlemen here represented three only
survive—Earl Russell, .Earl Stanhope, and
Viscount Eversley. The number of visitors
to the gallery last year was 63,195.

The Giornale di _Firenze relates the follow-
ing anecdote :—" The Princess Clotilda, sister
of King Amadeo of Spain, still inhabits
Prangins. As she is a very pious woman,
she often goes to Geneva and takes the sacra-
ment at Notre-Dame. About a fortnight ago
she arrived early at the church, according to
custom, and saw that a service was about to
commence at the altar of the Holy Virgin.
To approach the chapel and hear the mass
afforded great pleasure to the Princess.
Nevertheless, she remarked that several per-
sons were watching her. She wished to know
the (muse, and learnt that the mass she had
attended was celebrated, at the request of the
Duchess of Madrid, for the triumph of the
Carlists in Spain, and of course for the down-
fall of her own brother."

The trial of Stokes, who assassinated James
Fisk jun., on the stairs of the °rand Central
Hotel, in Now York, in January last, is now
proceeding.

The annual fete in aid of the Great Western
Railway Servants Widows' and Orphans'
Fund, &c., will take
.place this year on the
9th, at Nuneham Park, Oxford, one of the
loveliest spots for a pie-nic that can be found
in England, and easily accessible from all parts
of the Great Western Railway. The company
have generously offered the public unusual
advantages, and a brilliant and numerous
gathering may be anticipated. It is now
several years since the annual gathering took
place at Nuneham.

Dr. Lankester, the coroner for Central Mid-
dlesex, held an inquest on the 28th ult., at
the Crown Tavern, Goldington-creseent, to
investigate the circumstances attending the
death or Mrs. Fanny Hawker, aged 56 years,
who was 'found by the police in an insensible
state during the late severe storm. After
hearing the evidence, the jury returnel a
verdict of death from an effusion of blood on
the brain, brought on by excitement.

It appears from tho Bombay Gazette that
the heat continues to be exceptionally great
in India. At Allahabad it has reached 115
&gees in the shade, and at Hyderabad 116
degrees. At the latter place it caused the
death of an officer, four men, and 12 children
among the 16th Lancers. In and around
Poona, in the Deccan, the wells are dried up,
the cattle are dying, and people are thankful
if they can obtain a jar of water by no greater
trouble than that of walking a number of
miles for it. The Bombay Gazette says that
prospects would be very gloomy were not the
monsoon at hand.

An action, which occupied the Court of c
Queen's Bench three days in hearing, was
brought by the Bank of Egypt to recover,.
£3,650, the amount of a bill of exchange,
from Mr. Bassett, who had allowed Ca.rbonaro,
the manager of the bank, to draw on him to
that amount for the purchase of certain pro-
missory notes. Carbonaro's proceeding WO
found to be fraudulent, and payment of the
bill was refused. The bank, however, repu-
diated the proceedings of their manager and
claimed payment, but the Court decided in
favour of the defendant. In a cross action
brought by Mr. Bassett against the bank for a
set-off of .£2OO, the jury gave a verdict for the
bank.

A curious case, involving the validity of ft
Gretna Green marriage, came before the
Probate Court. It was alleged that a woman
was married at Gretna Green to a man named
her, and afterwards married another man
named Wilson. At her death Ker claimed her
estate ; but the jury, without leaving the box,
decided for Wilson, and ordered letters of.
administration to pass to him.

From Madrid we learn that the members of
the majority in the late Spanish Parliament,
including the former Ministers, have resolved
to take no part in the forthcoming elec-
tions. The Federal Republicans have deter g
mined to adopt the same course, and they
furthermore pledge themselves to oppose Mon-
archical Government of every kind, and
.to
acknowledge no authority noting in its
name.

News from the Persian Gulf states that the
hopes of a good barveiit have been realised,
and that corn is now selling at a comparatively
low rate. From the interior, however, no im-
provement is reported. The people at Teheran
and Ispahan are still severely suiferinc, from
famine. The correspondent of a Bombay
paper, writing from Ilushire, says that the
misery of the poor is most intense, and that
human beings have again been killed and
eaten. A correspondent of the Levant Tintes,
makes a similar statement.
•

Brazil having under instructions from his ao-,
vernment, issued a notice inviting British emi-
grants to settle in that country,theEmigration
Commissioners have been directed by her
Majesty's Government to publish information
for the use of intending emigrants. The
Commissioners point out that none other than,
"good agricultural emigrants" should go to
Brazil, as the only persons who succeed there
as artisans are Portuguese and Italians. The
emigrants, on arrival, are to be located in
colonies, and rural lands are to be assigned
to them in lots varying from 125,000 square

garden-party
at Lambeth Palace, was the
Indian chief Bunkwujjenene, of the Chippowiti,
Indian tribe, on the borders of Lake Superior,
The
accompanied by the Hey. E. F. Wilsofl.
chief is a line built man in the prirne. of life,
and, from wearing his native garb, attractca
considerable attention. His eXp012903 over

A sad accident, says the Swiss Tinos,
happened at Ependes on Monday evening. A
railway employe, 33 years of age, laid himself
down to sleep between the metals and was
killed by a train, which in passing over him,
cut his body into little pieces.

A horrible story is told by the New York
Times. It is said that a white woman in
Alabama, having married a near°, a party of
whites surprised the house, killed the husband
on, the spot, and burnt the wife alive by tying
her to the bed, saturating that and the clothes
with turpentine; and then setting fire to the
house. The account adds that after the
perpetrators had been arrested, several de-
t mined attempts were made to rescue them,
in one of which attempts a gaoler was
murdered.

A. brutal outrage was committed a few days
ago by a German, named Osterehamp on a
young girl named Christina Farkens, to whom
he wished to pay his addresses, but who refused
to have anything to say to him. Osterchamp
resides near Avoca, and about 15 miles from
the house of Miss Farkens. Early, one
morning Osterehamp rode across to the farm
of Mr. Farkens, assaulted him, and knocked
down with an axe two men who came to, his
assistance. He then chased Miss Farkens to
the house of a neighbouring farmer, tried to
bit her with an axe, but, failing in that,
knocked her down, broke her jaw bone, tried
to pull her teeth • out, and jumped upon her
until she became insensible. The fellow was
pursued by the neighbours, who arrested him,
and be is now awaiting trial. Miss Farkens,
though at one time in great danger, is now
recovering.—Melbourne Argus, April 23.

On the morning of the 28th ult, a most
destructive lire broke out at the button factory
of Messrs. W. Guest and Sons, Sheffield, The
building consisted of three storeys. The
rooms on the ground floor were used as the
boring and turning shop, the top storey as the
finishing room, and the second floor, and
rapidly spread through the building, com-
pletely gutting the two upper storeys, and
doing damage to the amount of several thou-
sand pounds. The factory gave employment
to over sixty hands,

A serious railway accident happened on the
29th ult. at the Middleton Junction Station,
but, fortunately, no lives were lost. By the
breaking of an axletree aetveral waggons of a
goods train were brought into violent contact
with the platform. Much damage was done to
the station, to the rolling stook, and to the
goods in transit.

Orders of her Majesty in Connell were pub-
lished in the Gazette of the 28th of June,
sanctioning bye-laws for the compulsory at-
tendance of children at school, made with the
approval of the Education Department.

Much excitement has been caused in county
Waterford by the elopement of the wife of a
gentlemen belonging to a distinguished and
ancient family, with a young English officer.
On Sunday the husband arrived in Dublin in
pursuit.

On the 29th, Mr. A. 3. Mandella, M.P.,
attended a conference of teachers of Hallam-
shire and district, the Mayor of Sheffield
presiding. Mr. Munciella spoke at great
length in favour of compulsory education, and
of the position of the teachers being hnproved
by the scholastic profession being made an
open career. He also coinpared the continental
schools with those of England, to the disadvan-
tage of the latter.

The Duke of Sutherland, accompanied by
Mr. Pender, M.P., has just paid a short visit
to the Isle of Man in order, to inspect the pro-
posed lines of railways which are about to be
constructed between Douglas, Pool, Port Erin,
and Ramsey. The ducal party was received
with great eclat and much public rejoicing,
and took their departure from the island highly
gratified with their visit.

-On the 29th ult, a camp of instruction
under the new regulation was opened for the
London Scottish Rifles on Wimbledon Com-
mon, and will lest to the end of the week.
The ScOtehmen went down in large numbers
in the afternoon and pitched their tents inside
the, ground enclosed for the National. Rifle
Association. Meeting, and the duties of min)
life were entered on with spirit. A camp of
instruction for the Tower Hamlets Volunteers
will be opened at Ilford on the 26th inst.' and
another one at Willesden for the Bloomsbury
Volunteers on the 29th inst.

About midday on the 28th, while five miners
were driving a heading in a pit 120 yards
deep, situated near Bilston, a piece of rook
was dislodged from the roof, and water poured
in from an old working. One of the men,
who had a wife and five children, was dosed
up in the gate road. The others, however,
escaped. Men were engaged till a late hour
in trying to rescue the poor man, but without
